title: Netflix Titus Adds Single-Tenant VM Isolation for Containers
gist: Netflix added single-tenant Titus, running one task per right-sized EC2 instance for performance isolation after concluding shared-kernel tuning cannot fully stop noisy neighbors; microVMs and gVisor were rejected.

insights.claim: Netflix concluded that cgroups, seccomp, iocost and traffic shaping cannot partition last-level cache and memory bandwidth, and the HTB shaper's global lock lets packet floods starve neighbors.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Shared-kernel multi-tenancy has hard performance limits for stateful, high-throughput jobs.
insights.quote: Netflix concluded that shared-kernel tuning narrows the gap without closing it.
insights.locator: Titus launches millions of containers a week

insights.claim: Titus launches millions of containers a week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances and is multi-tenant by default.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Scale reference for Netflix's compute platform.

insights.claim: Netflix rejected Firecracker/Kata (nested virtualization not ready, no GPU support, overhead), gVisor (I/O overhead, single-vendor maintenance) and plain EC2 (hands patching back to app teams).
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Shows practical limits of microVM and sandbox options in AWS today.

insights.claim: Netflix argues its workloads need performance isolation, not defense against hostile tenants.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Distinguishes performance from security isolation, which most competing offerings target.

insights.claim: Single-tenant mode uses an allowlist, smallest-fit instance autoscaling, pod anti-affinity, a non-preemptible priority class, a node taint and disabled defragmentation to enforce one task per node.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Replicable pattern for shared Kubernetes platforms: dedicated node pools with taints and no repacking.

insights.claim: Launch latency is the main cost, as a fresh instance needs tens of seconds to boot and warm pools help less due to many instance shapes; Netflix dropped metal instances for these pools.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Latency-sensitive starts bear the cost of right-sizing.
insights.locator: Launch latency is the main cost

insights.claim: Efficiency can improve by removing anti-affinity spreading that left shared hosts partly empty, but sidecar overhead can cost small instances tens of percent of resources.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Cost impact depends on instance size, favoring large workloads.

insights.claim: Netflix recommends the mode only for large, long-running, disruption-sensitive workloads sized near a node shape, with first users including managed Apache Flink, streaming connectors and telemetry pipelines.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Adoption limited to stateful streaming niches.
insights.locator: Early users include managed Apache Flink

insights.claim: Competing approaches include Instance-per-Pod Webhook, AWS Fargate, GKE sole-tenant nodes and GKE Sandbox, and Azure Pod Sandboxing, most targeting security isolation from untrusted code.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Landscape map of pod-level isolation offerings across clouds.
insights.locator: Single-tenant Titus joins a broader set

insights.claim: For the shared fleet Netflix is working on eBPF-based Expected Departure Time shaping, cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning via Intel RDT and AMD PQoS, NVIDIA MIG and cgroup v2 IO control, aiming for one Compute API that picks placement from declared intent.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Hardware partitioning features are the long-term fix for noisy neighbors.
